title: Jewish Communities Wiki
summary: Lead a medieval Jewish community: build its institutions, preserve its learning, and negotiate its place in the wider world.
body:
Jewish Communities, also called Kehillah, is a Crusader Kings III mod about the life of a Jewish diaspora community. You govern people and institutions within a host realm, rather than a territorial county.

A different kind of campaign

Your community needs a livelihood, trusted leadership, a working relationship with its host, and a living tradition of study. These concerns meet in three pillars: Affluence, Stability, and Greatness. Older records call Affluence Prosperity.

A wealthy community can lend, trade, and support its neighbours; a learned one can establish an academy and shape the reception of books; a politically skilled leader can secure privileges and protection. None of these removes the need to attend to the others.

Explore the wiki

  • What’s new in 0.2.0 and a playthrough as Rashi, with screenshots.
  • Getting started: installation and your first year.
  • Community government, pillars, and the Quarter.
  • Libraries, scholarship, and writing a sefer.
  • Host relations, crises, and migration and founding.
  • The book catalog and building reference, generated from the mod.

Which build does this describe?

This is a development wiki, last reviewed on 26 November 2026 for the 0.2.0 pre-alpha. The mod is in pre-alpha. A feature implemented in source may still await a live test, and the Workshop upload can lag behind development. Each article links to the records used to write it; the status page explains the distinction.

title: What's new in 0.2.0
summary: The 0.2.0 pre-alpha: new screens, Quarter slots, Great Works, the judges' vote, mutual aid, and more.
body:
0.2.0 is the second pre-alpha. It targets CK3 1.21 (Florin). Start a new game: saves from 0.1.1 may not work. Much of it has been checked in source but has had little live play, so please report problems.

New screens

The Domain, Laws, and Community Safety screens are now dashboards. Each pillar card names what is raising or lowering it. Reminders that used to be decisions are now top-bar alerts. The Prosperity pillar is now called Affluence. See community government and pillars.

The Jewish Quarter

Choose what goes in the Quarter's building slots: Market, Workshop, Bankers' Row, or Funduq. Upgrading the Synagogue opens up to three slots, and the Kahal House limits how many kinds you can run. Annex buildings such as the Hospital and the Court Jew's Office add more. Every building level has new painted art, in Western and Middle Eastern styles. The Quarter now appears as a district in its host city, adds to its economy, and needs goods from its market. See the Quarter.

Books and writing

  • Writing sparks: mastering a book can give you an idea. Develop it, then write it.
  • Great Works: meet their requirements to write one of about fifty historical books, or a lasting work of your own.
  • Wear and repair: library copies wear out. Mend them or lay them in the genizah.
  • News of new books: readers may study a new book, ban it, or travel to meet its author.
  • Missing foundational works: a top-bar notice names them, and a decision acquires one.

See writing a sefer, libraries, and the Rashi playthrough.

Law and learning

At the Bet Din you choose an argument and a source, then watch each judge vote. Ordained judges sit first. Nearby sages are invited, and guests choose what to do at the court, such as study or seek ordination. 100 new hearings have been added. She'elot let you send a legal question to a respected community; following its rulings can draw you toward its rite. They replace the old responsa letters. See the Bet Din.

Community life and money

Mutual aid lets you ransom captives, send relief, take in refugees, and appeal for help. It replaces the old loan ledger. You can lend to indebted rulers, demand repayment, and enforce bonds. You can run trade routes and invest in voyages through the Funduq. A community with a Hospital can send its court physician to an ill ruler. Jewish merchants and adventurers can belong to a home community and pay it a tithe. Members judge you by your record in office. See trade, lending, and mutual aid.

Faith

Jewish rites now keep kashrut, and the Quarter buys cattle for its meat. The herald of redemption adds a Jewish path to the messianic hope. Synods have three agenda topics: tenets, rite practice, and leadership. Every delegate's vote is shown.

Other changes

  • The Council has new tasks: three or four for each office.
  • Leadership styles reward your own actions and have new bonuses.
  • Lifestyle perks meant for landed rulers now give community bonuses.
  • The yeshiva stands in your Quarter. Former students can repay you, and its fame draws people.
  • An invitation letter names the county on offer, and you answer in the letter. You may lead the settlers yourself.
  • You can petition your ruler directly to name a Head of the Jews, and see your chances.
  • A crisis has one danger rating, and an alert for each action you can take.
  • The Kehillah start screens are the default, and communities begin without a standing army.

The full change log is in the 0.2.0 release notes.

title: Getting started
summary: Installation, compatibility, and a practical first-year checklist.
body:
Install and choose a playset

The current development descriptor targets CK3 1.21 (Florin). Subscribe to the pre-alpha Workshop item if you have access, enable Jewish Communities in the launcher, and use a playset containing only this mod while testing. Avoid enabling a local development copy and the Workshop copy together.

The release guide records that no DLC is required on 1.21: landless adventurers are available in the base game. Optional DLC supplies some additional content. Save compatibility between pre-alpha updates is not guaranteed; a new campaign gives the clearest test of new history and initialization.

Pre-alpha Workshop item. Availability follows the item’s current visibility and your access.

Your first campaign

Worms in 1066 is the recommended introduction. It has established institutions and a yeshiva, and has received more testing than the 867 and 1178 starts. Troyes offers a more demanding scholarly campaign; Granada puts host politics and communal danger at the centre.

  1. Pause and open Domain. Read the three pillar breakdowns and inspect the Quarter.
  2. Appoint the communal council. Match each officer’s skill to the office and read the available tasks.
  3. Review the host, settlement policy, charter, and Community Safety panel.
  4. Choose a leadership style and inspect the succession candidates.
  5. Open the library. Identify texts your rite treats as foundational, then select an attainable study project.
  6. Keep a reserve for unexpected costs before beginning a large construction programme.

What should I watch?

Read community news and suggested actions. A succession, charter renewal, dangerous agitator, empty council seat, or ripe writing spark may call for action. Your community’s survival and leadership are distinct from the fortunes of your dynasty: this is an appointed communal office.

For missing options and unexpected behaviour, consult the FAQ. Include your start date and mod build when reporting a bug.

title: Bookmarks and campaign choices
summary: The three historical settings and the kinds of campaign they offer.
body:
867: Age of the Geonim

The early start places the Babylonian academies, Masoretic scholarship, Mediterranean communities, and Jewish travellers in a world before many of the best-known Rishonim. The release guide’s roster includes Amram Gaon of Sura, Moshe ben Asher of Tiberias, Shefatiah of Oria, Kalonymus of Lucca, Hananel of Kairouan, Eldad ha-Dani, and the landed Khazar ruler Manasseh.

Later books are generally unavailable until their circulation dates. This gives an early campaign a different intellectual landscape, rather than merely fewer buildings.

1066: Age of the Rishonim

CampaignCharacter and setting
WormsIsaac ben Eliezer ha-Levi; an established Rhineland community and the recommended introduction.
TroyesShlomo Yitzhaki, Rashi; a small community with a strong scholarly focus.
GranadaJoseph ibn Naghrilla; office, influence, resentment, and a dangerous political setting.
FezYitzhak Alfasi, the Rif; North African learning and regional change.
David ben HezekiahA landless claimant with Davidic ancestry and a claim to Baghdad.

1178: The Paths of Torah

The later setting includes Maimonides in Fustat, Shmuel ben Eli in Baghdad, the Ri at Troyes, Yehuda he-Hasid at Speyer, the Raavad at Posquières, and Yosef ibn Shoshan at Toledo. A larger inherited literature and different scholarly traditions change the available paths.

Historical representation

Bookmark characters are selected points of entry, not an exhaustive list of playable communities. Historical documentation varies considerably between places and people. Authored personalities, exact institutional arrangements, and some map placements are gameplay reconstructions. The scenario and research records distinguish attested facts from inference.

The 867 and 1178 starts have received less testing than 1066. Rosters may change as the historical setup develops.

title: Playthrough: Rashi writes a commentary
summary: Troyes, 1066: a screenshot tour of the Quarter, library, Bet Din and writing chain as Shlomo Yitzhaki.
body:
Rashi, Rav Shlomo ben Yitzhak, starts the 1066 bookmark at 26, at the head of the small Kehillah of Troyes. This page follows one development-build session in which he studies, sits as judge, and writes a commentary on the Talmud. The screenshots are from that session.

The community at the start

Open the Domain tab first. Troyes starts in good health: Affluence and Stability are Healthy, and danger is Calm. Greatness, the pillar a scholar cares about most, starts Strained. The bottom strip shows that the community lives under King Philippe, whose outlook is Indifferent.

The Laws tab shows the charter with the host. At the start it is Fair: free to build, no communal watch, appeal to the king, unrestricted study, and customary tribute. No leadership style has been chosen yet.

Books before writing

A writer needs a shelf and the learning to use it. Rashi's Learning window lists the works he has mastered, in the order he learned them. A top-bar notice warns that the library lacks works foundational to its rite, here the Mishnah and two orders of the Bavli. The lack weighs on Greatness. Clicking the notice opens Acquire a Foundational Work.

A sitting of the Bet Din

A scholar-leader is also the community's judge. Community Safety's Host a Bet Din opens the activity planner. In this sitting, Rashi heard three cases. In one, a shofar had cracked before a public service, and the court had to decide whether that service still counted.

Writing the commentary

Writing begins with a spark, an idea that comes from mastering a book. Developed far enough, a Talmudics spark becomes a Great Work. Write a Sefer then asks what to write.

The writing ran from November 1066 to June 1068. Rashi gathered evidence with his chavrusa, Judah, and later had to answer a fellow scholar's objection. He could defend the passage, narrow the claim, or take another season to rebuild the chapter. Each option's tooltip gives its cost.

The new work enters the Ledger of Sefarim with one copy and one master, its author. Like every new work, it starts Obscure. Its quality placed it at 38 of the 40 points needed for Popular, and its rite could one day hold it Authoritative. Word of the book then spread to other communities.

Troyes on the map

About this session

This was a development build of 26 November 2026. To reach writing within one session, console debug events supplied the mastered Talmud orders and the Great Work spark, which normally come from years of study. Rashi's own historical commentary needs four orders of the Bavli mastered, and he had three, so the book was written as an original Great Work instead. See the writing guide for how the system is meant to work.

title: Community government and households
summary: The Kehillah, its landless title, householders, and communal institutions.
body:
What you govern

A Kehillah is a self-governing Jewish community located within another ruler’s realm. Its title represents communal leadership; its Jewish Quarter is its physical seat. The community is not the county, and the host continues to govern the surrounding territory.

The leader is commonly styled Parnas, or Rav if ordained. Offices such as Nagid and Gaon represent additional roles with their own requirements; a high scholarly title does not automatically make its holder the territorial ruler.

Households

The community’s Jewish families form its social base. Householder heads, or ba’alei batim, contribute through their occupations and standing. A scholar, merchant, or advocate supports a different aspect of communal life. Household recruitment therefore affects more than court size.

Prosperity and capacity influence the community’s ability to accommodate people. Hardship and danger can push families away; settlement and refugee arrivals can replenish them. Household recruitment can bring spouses and children, rather than only isolated skilled courtiers.

Your main tools

  • Domain: the community’s pillars, leadership style, and Quarter.
  • Council: officers working on revenue, construction, host relations, protection, law, and learning.
  • Library and Learning: communal books, personal mastery, and writing ideas.
  • Community Safety: local danger and an active crisis.
  • The community and world ledgers: other seats, their leaders, and wider communal standing.

The dashboards

The Laws tab collects the leadership style, the charter with the host and its terms, and the succession and gender laws. Community Safety has its own dashboard; see danger and recovery.

The Jewish Communities map mode shows every community. A community’s card gives its leader, pillars, and danger, with shortcuts to its host, Quarter, and library.

Leadership is an office

The community appoints its next leader through its own succession system. Your family can remain influential without automatically inheriting the office. Build institutions that will endure beyond the incumbent, and inspect succession before a transition becomes urgent.

Leaving communal leadership can open a landless campaign. Realm-wide Jewish offices have their own eligibility and should not be treated as permanent possessions after stepping down.

title: Affluence, Stability, and Greatness
summary: The three measures of communal health and how to read their breakdowns.
body:
PillarRepresentsTypical concerns
AffluenceMaterial resources and economic lifeHouseholds, trade, income, construction, lending, and relief
StabilityCommunal cohesion and securityJustice, trust, protection, disputes, and danger
GreatnessLearning and communal distinctionBooks, scholars, academies, religious life, and reputation

Older documentation and many internal script names call Affluence Prosperity. They refer to the same pillar family.

Bands and change over time

Pillars are grouped into bands from Crisis through Legendary. The band matters for opportunities, buildings, and the community’s condition. A pillar’s current value and its baseline are different: institutions and circumstances support a level toward which the community moves, while particular actions can produce more immediate changes.

Hover the pillar to inspect its contributors. A temporary accomplishment can remain valuable after its original officer changes tasks, then expire later. Read the contributor’s duration as well as its size.

Leadership and expectations

A leadership style favours the corresponding pillar and candidate skills. The current style values retire the old flat +60 baseline bonus: positive actions on the mandate pillar receive a 20% boost instead. Do not add the old bonus when planning a build.

The community also records the condition inherited by a leader and its high-water marks. Leadership is judged in relation to those expectations, with extra emphasis on the mandate pillar. This records a tenure’s performance; it does not make all three pillars interchangeable currencies.

Practical priorities

Inspect a weak pillar’s actual causes before spending resources. Missing foundational texts are a Greatness concern only when they are foundational in your community’s rite. Revenue may help fund protection, but an unresolved political grievance is not answered by a library upgrade.

Severe, sustained instability can threaten the community’s survival. Treat warnings as calls to intervene and preserve resources for recovery.

title: The Jewish Quarter
summary: Core institutions, specialisations, annexes, and construction permissions.
body:
Institutions and specialisations

The current Quarter redesign distinguishes essential communal institutions from a limited choice of specialisations. The Synagogue anchors the Quarter. The Beit Midrash supports study and can develop into a yeshiva; the Kahal House supports administration; the Hekdesh supports charity and care.

Specialisations give a community a more particular character: the Kosher Market, Bankers’ Row, Craft Row, Funduq, and Wall and Gates compete for available capacity. Annexes add facilities within a larger institution. You are choosing a community’s priorities, rather than completing an identical list everywhere.

InstitutionPrincipal role
SynagoguePrayer, communal religious life, and associated facilities
Beit MidrashStudy, library activity, and higher teaching
Kahal HouseCommunal administration and capacity
HekdeshHospitality, poor relief, and recovery
Kosher Market / Craft Row / FunduqLocal provisioning, production, and commerce
Bankers’ RowLending and financial expertise
Wall and GatesPhysical protection, subject to permission

Building slots

Since 0.2.0, the Synagogue’s upgrades open up to three building slots. Fill each with a Market, Workshop, Bankers’ Row, or Funduq. The Kahal House limits how many kinds you can run at once. Annexes such as the Hospital and the Court Jew’s Office attach to a larger building. The Quarter is also a district of its host city: it adds to the city’s economy and needs goods from its market.

Every building level has painted art, in Western and Middle Eastern styles, with terrain backgrounds and seasonal and Jerusalem variants.

Building conditions

Read the actual construction tooltip. Costs, pillar gates, parent tiers, space, and the host charter can all matter. A right to build freely differs from construction by permission; a temporary permit may be necessary. Fortifying the Quarter can require a separate right.

A scribe’s room or workshop is not automatically a functioning manuscript-copying operation. The relevant upgraded scribal facility must be available. See libraries for acquisition routes.

Development status

The core-and-specialisation redesign is implemented in development source, with several layout and trade integrations still awaiting live checks. Earlier screenshots and release guides show the previous separate building lines. The generated building reference lists definitions in the source used for this wiki build, including any retained legacy entries; it is not a promise that every definition can be constructed.

title: Council and communal officers
summary: What each council seat does and how the redesigned tasks support the community.
body:
The five seats

OfficeSkillResponsibility
ShtadlanDiplomacyRepresentation before the host and goodwill outside the community
GabbaiStewardshipRevenue, building, fairs, and tzedakah
Rosh ha-ShmirahMartialThe Quarter’s defence, travellers, and revenue farming
Ne’emanIntrigueTrust, secrets, and the pledge chest
DayyanLearningLaw, teaching, study, and the Bet Din

Since 0.2.0, each office has three or four tasks, each with its own icon. A task’s tooltip gives its chance and effect for the officer you appointed.

The host and the neighbourhood

Petition the Host concerns the ruler’s opinion, settlement policy, outlook, and charter. Cultivate Goodwill, formerly Seek Protection, concerns people around the community: Stability, religious restraint, and relations across faiths. These tasks answer different sources of insecurity.

Money, trade, and charity

The Gabbai can raise communal revenue, oversee construction, trade at fairs, or manage tzedakah. The fairs support economic relations and cultural acceptance; tzedakah connects local religious life with mutual aid. Construction work can also help after violence.

The Rosh ha-Shmirah can defend the Quarter, escort travellers, or farm the lord’s revenues. Revenue farming brings income and goodwill from the lord, but can intensify popular hostility. Its returns and risks depend on the town’s mood: an angry town is both less profitable and more dangerous.

Learning and justice

The Dayyan’s work links teaching, study partnership, and court preparation to systems you actively use. Teach the Community can produce Greatness accomplishments; Learn in Chavruta makes the Dayyan available as a study partner and helps book acquisition. Prepare the Bet Din gives the court more time before it is considered overdue.

Accomplishments last beyond the task

The three pillar tasks can create named, time-limited accomplishments recorded in community news and the pillar breakdown. Their benefits can outlast the officer’s assignment. Higher skill improves the chances; merely assigning a task does not grant every possible accomplishment at once.

Court positions such as Rosh Yeshiva, Sofer, Shochet, Gabbai Tzedakah, and Mikvah Attendant are separate from the five-seat council. Their availability depends on the relevant institution and eligibility.

The redesigned task set is source-built as of 25 November; the latest tooltips and outcomes still require live verification.

title: Leadership styles and succession
summary: Appointment, endorsements, leadership mandates, and continuing after a leader’s death.
body:
Appointment rather than inheritance

Kehillah leadership uses a merit-based appointment system. Candidate skills, scholarly qualifications, piety, family standing, and endorsements contribute to the choice. Being the incumbent’s child does not guarantee succession.

Inspect the candidates and their score breakdowns while you can still influence the field. Endorsing someone helps within this system; it does not replace all eligibility rules or guarantee the result.

Choose a mandate

Domain offers Scholarly, Political, and Commercial leadership. The community holds the mandate, including its ten-year commitment, so a new leader does not automatically reset it. Selecting a style does not remove the incumbent.

StyleCandidate emphasisArea of action
ScholarlyLearningGreatness and scholarly institutions
PoliticalDiplomacyStability, influence, and protection
CommercialStewardshipAffluence, trade, and finance

The current values strengthen positive actions on the corresponding pillar by 20%. The older +60 baseline is retired. Recent development also adds style-specific opportunities, including profit-route capacity, political schemes, and scholarly court/follower advantages. Read your build’s style tooltip for the current set.

When a leader leaves office

The intended communal campaign continues through its chosen successor, even outside the previous leader’s dynasty. Stepping down instead can lead to a landless adventurer campaign. Eligibility for a realm Jewish office must be reconsidered when communal leadership ends.

Cherem can put a leader’s office at risk. The implemented follow-up offers a teshuva route before forced abdication and removes inappropriate retained realm offices. These changes have separate live-test requirements.

Testing limits

Succession and government laws have caused crashes during development. A source check establishes the intended rules, not that every transition works in a live save. Report a failed continuation with the save, leader, selected successor, and build.

title: Libraries and the Sefarim Ledger
summary: Ownership, acquisition, mastery, and the standing of books in each rite.
body:
Three different questions

  • Ownership: does this community possess a copy?
  • Mastery: has this character studied the work successfully?
  • Standing: how does the selected rite regard it?

Owning a book does not make every resident its master. A celebrated manuscript artifact is also distinct from a work’s authority in a rite. The library, character learning, and artifact system represent related but different things.

Acquire a work

The Ledger provides routes to obtain eligible works. A nearby library, copying facilities, and distant scholarly networks offer different opportunities. A historical work can be available through those networks after its circulation date even if no registered community currently owns a copy. An unwritten future landmark is a different case.

Copying requires the appropriate scribal facility, not just any Beit Midrash. Greyed-out choices can explain a missing prerequisite. Compare the actual requirement with the Quarter’s buildings and annexes.

Read the rite’s assessment

Sort by rank to see what matters most in the selected tradition. Highest attainable rank explains the current ceiling: the greatest standing the work can reach under that rite’s authority and tenet rules. It is a limit within the game’s reception system, not a universal judgment on the historical book.

Other traditions use a shorter comparison: Rejected, Unknown, Ambivalent, Important, or Holy. A book may be foundational in one rite and controversial in another. Missing Bavli orders should not penalize a community whose rite does not treat them as foundational; harmful books can still have their own consequences.

Missing foundational works

Each rite treats some works as foundational. If any are missing from the shelf, a top-bar notice names them, and the community’s Greatness suffers until they are acquired. Click the notice, or take Acquire a Foundational Work, to seek a copy of one.

Wear and repair

Library copies wear out with use and age. Mend a worn copy, or lay one beyond repair in the genizah, as tradition requires for a sacred text.

Movement and survival

A collection belongs to more than its current building. The county-endowment implementation preserves collection and study references when a suitable Jewish temple becomes its seat, with a Quarter fallback if necessary. Crises and expulsion can endanger books; copying and protective institutions matter.

Use the generated catalog for authors, languages, and configured dates. In-game gates remain authoritative for an individual campaign.

title: Study, rabbis, and yeshivot
summary: The three disciplines, language, mastery, study partnerships, and ordination.
body:
Three disciplines

DisciplineFocus
ParshanutScriptural interpretation, commentary, and related literature
TalmudicsTalmud, halakhic reasoning, and legal scholarship
MachshavahJewish thought, philosophy, theology, and esoteric traditions

The Rabbi trait records scholarly development across these tracks. Learning skill and Learning lifestyle experience are separate from disciplinary progress and mastery of a particular work.

Study a sefer

Select a work through the library or the relevant study flow. Learning, the work’s difficulty, language, and the reader’s tradition affect what is possible and how successful study will be. The study-timing revision aims for projects on the order of months rather than routine multi-year reading, with the actual duration modified by the reader.

Hebrew, Aramaic, and other literary languages matter. A character can own a work whose language remains difficult. A chavrusa provides a study partnership and can improve the project; council tasks and scholarly contacts can help make that partnership available.

Mastery has uses

Mastered works support legal argument, teaching, writing, and other scholarly actions. First mastery can also produce an Insight in the appropriate discipline. Acquiring a long shelf without studying it does not supply those personal qualifications.

The yeshiva

A yeshiva is a seat of higher teaching with a head, students, and a teaching focus. Students enrol, travel, and study with a rebbe and study partner. The ordination system develops scholars over time rather than making everyone at a learned court a rabbi immediately.

A community card’s Yeshiva label opens the same library entry point and can show its head, student count, and subject in the tooltip. A temple can also matter as an institutional seat where the relevant systems allow it.

Religious differences

Access to ordinary Jewish library study does not universally require a Rabbinic Oral Torah tenet. Non-Rabbinic readers retain their own scriptural and scholarly traditions. Do not assume that a Karaite, Samaritan, or Haymanot character receives the same Talmudics advantages or canon as a Rabbinic scholar.

title: Writing a sefer
summary: From a study-born Insight to a Chiddush, a Great Work, and a finished manuscript.
body:
Ideas come from study

A new campaign begins without writing sparks. First mastery of a sefer can offer an Insight related to that work, with one active slot in each discipline: Parshanut, Talmudics, and Machshavah. A competing idea may ask you to keep the existing one or replace it. Sparks do not fade simply because time passes.

Three tiers

TierMeaning
InsightAn initial idea, suitable for a smaller writing project
ChiddushA developed contribution, reached through further study or disciplinary work
Great WorkA project ready for an eligible, still-unfilled landmark niche

An Insight can deepen through aptitude growth, another mastered work, or an action appropriate to its discipline: a sermon, court ruling, responsum, debate, or chavrusa. Requirements count from the spark’s arrival where the system specifies that timing.

Open the Learning window’s Sparks tab. The Upgrade Spark tooltip lists the next rung’s requirements. For the player, meeting them makes an upgrade available; you choose to take it. A project form without a catalogued landmark niche can stop at Chiddush.

Begin the scheme

Use Write a Sefer or the card’s Write button, then select a held idea. Starting consumes that spark. Research, objections, partnership, and revision shape the manuscript’s quality and chance of completion. Language and Learning remain relevant even for a promising idea.

Revising the draft

A book takes a year or more to write. Events along the way ask how to gather evidence, for example with your chavrusa, and how to meet a fellow scholar’s objections. You can defend the passage, narrow the claim, or take another season to rebuild at the cost of Stress. Each option’s tooltip gives its effect.

What completion creates

The Manuscript’s Fate reports what the finish did:

  • the quality and its tier;
  • the spark the book came from;
  • its Ledger outcome;
  • whether it became a historical landmark, and if not, why not;
  • your chavrusa.

The option lists its reward. The manuscript artifact carries the work’s own name.

A Great Work that fits an open historical niche, and passes the landmark roll, takes that landmark’s place in history, with you as its author. Otherwise it can enter the Ledger as an original work under its own title. The report says whether a book entered the Ledger, was kept out because the slots were full, or remains a manuscript only.

Every new work starts Obscure. Its quality sets how close it starts to Popular. From there, copies, masters, and approbations raise its standing, up to the highest rank its rite allows.

Great Works

About fifty historical books have Great Work paths, each with its own requirements. Some historical authors have shorter routes to their own books. Any qualified scholar may write one, and the book then enters history under that scholar’s name. Readers who hear of a new book may study it, ban it, or travel to meet its author.

Development status

A live run on 26 November 2026 (the Rashi playthrough) confirmed the completion report, the manuscript’s name, and the Obscure starting rank. Rashi’s own Talmud commentary was not open to him in that run: its niche asks for four orders of the Bavli mastered, and he had three. The named historical routes still await a live test. Check the current card and project tooltip rather than an old ambition description.

title: Faiths, rites, and tenets
summary: Religious authority, regional traditions, personal commitments, and book reception.
body:
Faith and rite

A faith establishes broad religious commitments and authority. A rite represents a more particular tradition of practice and learning. The mod uses these distinctions to give communities different canons, institutions, and attitudes toward books without reducing all Jewish life to one interchangeable set of bonuses.

The represented traditions include Bavel, Ashkenaz, Sepharad, Yerushalmi, Yordei Merkavah, Karaite, Haymanot, Malabar, Samaritan, and Kabar traditions. Names and the balance of their cores continue to develop; use the in-game rite panel for your campaign’s current configuration.

Tenet standing

A tenet can be central to a rite, known and available, or forbidden under its faith’s rules. Personal adoption represents a character’s own commitment and can have separate benefits and actions. Sharing a faith does not mean every individual has personally adopted every available practice.

Authority doctrines answer a different question from personal preference. Personally adopting a scholarly tenet does not independently turn a non-Rabbinic authority into Rabbinic authority or make the Bavli its canon.

Names you may encounter

NameContext
Iyyun ha-TalmudThe Rabbinic display of Scholarly Study
Pesak HalakhaThe Rabbinic display of Religious Legal Pronouncements
Peshuto shel MiqraLiteralism in a Jewish context
HokhmahReasoned inquiry and philosophical learning
PiyyutSacred Liturgy in a Jewish context
Covenant CommunityThe Jewish solidarity treatment developed from the earlier Communal Identity implementation

Books and disputes

Tenets influence scholarly action and the reception of works. A philosophical text can support one conviction and encounter resistance from another. The Ledger’s ceiling and stance explain those constraints; a book’s standing is not identical to its age, artifact rarity, or your personal admiration.

Synods can debate changes to communal religious life. The Gaonate, Sanhedrin, and existing Samaritan priesthood are distinct institutional systems, with their own historical and game rules.

Non-Rabbinic traditions

Karaites, Samaritans, Haymanot, and other traditions should not inherit Rabbinic texts, offices, or holiday assumptions indiscriminately. The authority and holiday revisions address those differences. Particular historical identifications remain subject to research and review.

title: The Bet Din and responsa
summary: Judges, cases, arguments, sources, and the wider network of legal learning.
body:
A court with consequences

The Bet Din is the community’s rabbinic court. Its sittings bring judges together to hear disputes and communal questions. Cases range from commercial agreements and dowries to captivity and other responsibilities. The parties and the ruling matter as well as the quality of the argument.

Prepare the bench

Qualified judges and relevant mastered sources improve the court’s resources. A book on a communal shelf and a judge who knows how to use it are different advantages. Council preparation, institutional facilities, and leadership style can influence the court’s timing or performance.

Convene a sitting when the decision’s requirements are met. Ordinary cooldowns and the point at which the court is overdue are distinct. Recent development makes scholarly leadership able to hold sittings more frequently and revises the Dayyan’s preparation task; use your build’s tooltip for the exact timing.

Hear and decide

Read the dispute, evaluate the available arguments, and consult the native outcome preview. Cite relevant sources when offered. A stronger case can change the probabilities without guaranteeing every desired result. Some bespoke cases also carry particular consequences beyond the general court result.

Argue and watch the vote

Since 0.2.0, you choose an argument and a source for each case. You can speak from your own judgment, or cite a work you have mastered. The option tooltip shows the odds. Each judge then votes, and the ruling shows who was persuaded.

Ordained judges sit first, and a lay bench sits when none is available. Nearby sages are invited. Guests choose an intent, such as study or seeking ordination. A sitting ends with a conclusion that names its guests, any citation offered, and whether the host’s intent succeeded.

Ask beyond the community

A difficult question can become a she’elah sent to a scholar elsewhere, with a responsum connecting local law to the wider scholarly network. This makes distant relationships and learned correspondents useful even without political control over their communities.

Development status

A full sitting was played live on 26 November 2026, from Community Safety’s Host a Bet Din, through three cases, to the conclusion. That run logged many tooltip errors while the argument options were on screen, so a value that looks blank or wrong there may be a bug: please report it. The she’elah system replaced the old responsa letters in 0.2.0.

title: Synods, Gaon, Nagid, and Sanhedrin
summary: How local leadership differs from religious and realm-wide offices.
body:
Different scales of authority

InstitutionScope
Parnas or RavLeadership of a particular Kehillah
NagidA realm-wide Jewish office associated with the host’s political order
GaonScholarly authority and academy leadership through the Gaonic system
Head of riteLeadership associated with a particular religious tradition
Sanhedrin / NasiA separate, difficult restoration route to a central institution
Samaritan High PriestA distinct existing priestly office

Synods

A synod brings communities into discussion about their rite and common religious life. The development agenda can cover marriage, belief, ordinances, headship, common undertakings, and a ban against a leader. Which matters appear depends on what is live in the participating tradition.

A question of belief presents relevant tenets and their standing, rather than a universal list without context. The latest dynamic agenda and picker are source-built and still require a live check.

Realm and scholarly offices

The Nagid’s relationship to a host realm differs from an academy’s authority. Losing community leadership can affect eligibility for realm offices. Likewise, recognition as Gaon is not simply the reward for owning a large library: the system considers appropriate authority and scholarly recognition.

Davidic descent and recognition as Exilarch are also distinct from possessing Baghdad. David ben Hezekiah’s claim supplies a possible campaign objective, not an automatic grant of its community.

Restoration is a project

The Sanhedrin route is deliberately exceptional. Its restoration, seat, and leadership have their own prerequisites and should not be confused with a generic create-head-of-faith action. A proposed Jerusalem High Priesthood is not implied by the existence of Temple Service or by the Samaritan office.

Priestly succession

The latest Samaritan succession revision gives the High Priest a Kohen-line appointment system. It is source-built but not yet live-tested; treat unexpected heirs as a succession bug requiring the save and build details.

title: Hosts, charters, and settlement policy
summary: The ruler, religious advisers, local opinion, and the rights of the community.
body:
Living under another ruler

The host controls the territory around the Quarter. Your relationship with that ruler matters, but personal opinion is only one part of it. Settlement policy, a charter’s terms, religious counsel, debts, grievances, and popular hostility can pull in different directions.

Settlement policy

Realms can ban, discourage, allow, or encourage Jewish settlement. AI rulers revisit their policy in response to their character and circumstances. Permission to reside does not automatically provide every commercial, judicial, or defensive privilege.

The charter

A charter records concrete terms such as construction, jurisdiction, markets, lending, and protection. Read each term rather than treating the document as a single friendly-or-hostile score. Renewal and changes of leadership are moments when privileges may need defending.

The Shtadlan’s Petition the Host task addresses the ruler and charter. Cultivate Goodwill builds support around the community and can encourage restraint from religious advisers. A ruler’s favour can coexist with a hostile town, and a well-disposed cleric can be valuable even when court politics are difficult.

Economic usefulness and resentment

Lending, trade, service, and tax collection can make the community valuable. They can also expose it to debt grievances or popular resentment. Farm the Lord’s Revenues makes this tradeoff explicit: the lord benefits, but local mood affects the income and danger.

Expulsion and conquest

An expulsion warning provides time to plead, pay, or prepare an orderly departure under the existing system. A change of host should trigger a reassessment of the community’s position. Not every proposed Jewish-conqueror outcome is implemented: the county-endowment library preservation work does not itself add the full choice to elevate a community leader after conquest.

Keep the distinction between communal violence, formal expulsion, and a territorial conquest. Each can threaten the Quarter through a different chain of events.

title: Danger, violence, and recovery
summary: Read the danger breakdown, respond during agitation, defend the Quarter, and recover.
body:
Before a crisis

Community Safety explains the sources of danger around the Quarter. Ruler hostility, popular pressure, agitation, and particular grievances are different contributors. Stability and protection help, but no single opinion number explains the whole situation.

Since 0.2.0, danger is one rating, from Calm upward, with a yearly chance. Each action you can take against it appears as a top-bar alert.

Agitation: a visible race

An active warning opens a crisis situation. During agitation, competing progress toward Armed Host and Spared represents escalation and successful restraint. Catalysts and monthly contributors identify what is moving the race. Read the bars and their sources; the system is not simply a concealed final die roll.

Prepare the watch, provisions, and a route out; answer accusations and seek effective protection where available. Many responses are limited by phase or have their own costs and skill checks. Starting preparation and receiving its completed benefit can happen at different times.

When an armed host gathers

The priority changes from preventing escalation to protecting people and the Quarter. Defence, negotiation, patronage, and communal funding can affect the outcome. Contributions buy additional protection with diminishing returns: inspect the marginal price of the next point rather than assuming every payment buys the same amount.

Outcomes

  • Spared: the escalation is averted.
  • Quarter Held: the community withstands the attack, though damage and aftermath can remain.
  • Quarter Struck: violence reaches the community, with losses and a recovery phase.

A breach can also change the ruler’s standing and policy toward Jews. A political settlement and the physical aftermath are related consequences, not substitutes for one another.

Recovery and neighbours

Repair buildings, care for victims, support displaced families, and restore communal life. Nearby communities can receive news and offer tzedakah, fasting, and other support. The available responses depend on how the crisis ended.

Preparation, solidarity, and reserves all matter. An outcome called Held or Spared does not mean every cost disappears immediately, and recovery actions can carry cooldowns.

Historical crises

Granada’s 1066 chain has authored historical circumstances. Its danger should not be read as a universal script for every Muslim host or a rule that all campaigns must repeat the historical outcome.

title: Trade, lending, and mutual aid
summary: Quarter income, economic specialisation, debt, and obligations to other communities.
body:
Income serves institutions

The community’s economy rests on households, the Quarter, trade, and its place in the host realm. Gold pays for construction, books, protection, and relief. Affluence also opens opportunities and creates expectations about what the community can contribute.

Specialise

Economic building choices support different livelihoods. Craft production, a market, a Funduq, and Bankers’ Row serve different combinations of goods, routes, and finance. Recent development connects craft trades and the winery and scribes to their own goods, while the Factor’s House supports route capacity and competitiveness.

Commercial leadership adds an economic emphasis, but does not remove the need for capable officers or favourable conditions. Escorting travellers can support Quarter income and commenda outcomes as well as safety.

Lending

The current lending implementation uses vanilla loans, with community identification and succession handling. Read the debtors panel and the actual loan terms. The faith’s usury doctrine and the borrower’s religious relationship affect which loans and terms are appropriate.

Banking can improve a ruler’s view of the community’s services; unpaid debts can also become a political grievance. The Keep the Pledge Chest task and financial specialisations support lending through their own benefits. Older custom-ledger and quarterly-repayment descriptions are superseded by the vanilla-loan integration.

Give and receive

Tzedakah and mutual aid link communities. A prosperous seat can support a poorer or threatened neighbour; hardship can make receiving help an immediate priority. Giving can bring communal standing, piety, and relationships, while relief helps the recipient recover.

The Gabbai’s charity task strengthens this role and adds religious benefits. Do not assume every gift grants every possible reward: the action, recipient state, and current build determine the result.

Mutual aid between communities

Since 0.2.0, mutual aid lets you ransom captives, send relief, take in refugees, and appeal to others for help. It replaces the old loan ledger. Letters from communities in need arrive with options to send your share, send what they still need, or refuse. Each choice’s tooltip gives its cost in standing and goodwill.

Other 0.2.0 additions: lend to rulers in debt, demand repayment, and enforce bonds; run trade routes and invest in voyages through the Funduq; send the Hospital’s physician to an ill ruler. Jewish merchants and adventurers can belong to a home community and pay it a tithe.

Risk and reserves

A highly profitable arrangement can create political exposure. Revenue farming is the clearest example: it can enrich the community and please the lord while making townspeople angrier. Keep enough liquidity to answer a crisis or repair losses rather than committing everything to the next tier.

title: Founding, migration, and adventurers
summary: Settle a new community, answer an invitation, visit an existing seat, or pursue a claim.
body:
A community can move or multiply

Landless Jewish adventurers can seek a place to settle, and existing communities can send settlers. A suitable location, local permission, resources, and the founding rules all matter. The mod limits communal seats rather than treating every unoccupied city as automatically available.

Invitations

Invitations can connect rulers seeking settlement, communities sending families, and adventurers looking for a home. Read the offered location, promises, resources, and eligibility carefully. An invitation is an opportunity to settle under particular conditions, not a grant of territorial rule.

A new county-specific letter flow is being revised in the shared development checkout. Its latest routing, travel discounts, and leader choices are not documented here as released features. Pledged joint foundations and additional lead-the-settlers options remain proposals.

Visit an established community

An eligible adventurer visiting a county with a Kehillah can encounter the community through the local visit flow. The leader can offer fellowship, settlement discussion, and introductions to households with scholarly, commercial, or practical skills. Recruitment can bring a family, not merely one worker.

Claims

A suitable claimant can pursue leadership of an existing community. David ben Hezekiah’s Baghdad claim is an authored example, but the interaction is designed for eligible claimants more generally. Recognition as Exilarch is a separate question from winning the seat.

Conquest and collections

A new territorial ruler does not automatically erase the community’s history. County endowment can relocate a library to a suitable temple while preserving references. The broader choice for a Jewish conqueror to elevate a leader remains separate work, rather than an assumed feature of every conquest.

title: Festivals and religious life
summary: Seasonal events, sermons, pilgrimage, liturgy, and the differences between traditions.
body:
A religious calendar

Festival events bring the year into the community’s life through choices, household encounters, and religious observance. The mod’s holiday content is a distinct family of events alongside the Kehillah government systems.

Different Jewish traditions do not share every observance in the same form. The faith, authority, and holiday revision gates content so that non-Rabbinic characters do not automatically receive Rabbinic assumptions. A familiar festival name is not evidence that every tradition follows identical practice.

Sermons and liturgy

Preaching links Learning and religious life to communal standing. Relevant mastered texts and commitments can support the activity. A sermon can also provide the disciplinary experience needed to deepen a Parshanut writing idea.

Piyyut represents sacred liturgical composition and performance. Its personal practice and religious benefits are distinct from canon: a prayer text does not become canonical merely because it is sung, and a non-Rabbinic worshipper should not be assigned a Rabbinic source indiscriminately.

Pilgrimage and sacred places

Sacred Homeland and related practices connect religious life to holy sites. The Temple Service implementation adds sacrifice intent through the pilgrimage framework, distinguishing Jerusalem from the Samaritan focus on Gerizim. This is conditional content with runtime checks still pending; it does not mean the Jerusalem Temple is restored at game start.

Belief in action

Reasoned inquiry, esoteric study, communal solidarity, messianic hope, and other commitments can have individual actions as well as follower benefits. Their availability depends on a character’s faith, rite, personal commitment, and the current circumstances.

Use Faiths, rites, and tenets to understand those layers. Religious flavour and mechanically available actions should be read together, with a proposal distinguished from an implemented practice.

title: FAQ and troubleshooting
summary: Missing actions, library questions, succession, updates, and useful bug reports.
body:
Why can’t I copy a manuscript?

A Beit Midrash is not necessarily an upgraded scribal workshop. Check the required copying facility, the available copy, resources, and the route’s other conditions. A disabled option’s tooltip should explain the remaining requirements.

Why is a book important elsewhere but weak in my rite?

Reception is rite-specific. Authority and tenets affect its standing and highest attainable rank. The Ledger’s Other traditions comparison is a shorthand, not a second personal mastery score.

Why didn’t my written book enter the Ledger?

Ordinary success produces a manuscript artifact and local news. A catalogued landmark needs a Great Work spark, an open niche, its particular requirements, and the appropriate outcome. An Insight or Chiddush alone cannot fill a landmark.

Why isn’t my child the successor?

The communal office uses appointment and merit. Family standing is one influence among others. Review eligible candidates, the leadership style, and endorsements.

Why doesn’t an old save show a new historical character or building setup?

History and some initialization run when a campaign begins. Pre-alpha saves are not guaranteed to migrate safely. Reproduce the issue in a new campaign when testing a changed start.

Why does the wiki describe something absent from my Workshop copy?

The wiki covers development, while Workshop uploads are staged releases. Some additions remain source-built and unverified. Check your release information and the linked implementation record.

Can I combine this with other mods?

Begin with Jewish Communities alone. Mods changing governments, religious systems, title history, or overlapping interface files can conflict. Add other mods only when you can identify compatibility, and remove them when reproducing a bug.

What makes a useful report?

  • CK3 version, mod build or release, and enabled DLC.
  • Start date, character, and whether the save was created before an update.
  • The action taken, the result, and what you expected.
  • Other enabled mods and whether the issue reproduces without them.
  • A save and relevant error-log excerpt where available. A screenshot helps for a rendering problem.

Report an issue on GitHub.

title: Glossary
summary: Common Hebrew and institutional terms used throughout the mod.
body:
Ba’al Bayit; ba’alei batim
A householder; the communal householders collectively.
Beit Midrash
A house of study.
Bet Din; batei din
A court; courts. In this mod, the communal rabbinic court system.
Chavrusa / chavruta
A study partnership, or one’s study partner.
Cherem / herem
A ban or excommunication, with particular conditions and consequences in the mod.
Chiddush
A developed scholarly insight; the middle tier of a writing spark.
Dayyan
A judge; the council officer responsible for law and learning.
Funduq
A commercial lodging or trading establishment, used for a Quarter specialisation.
Gabbai
A communal collector or administrator; the council’s financial officer.
Gaon; Geonim
A title associated particularly with the heads of the Babylonian academies; the mod models Gaonic recognition and institutions.
Hekdesh
In the Quarter, the institution for hospitality, poor relief, and care.
Kahal / Kehillah; kehillot
A community; communities.
Kohen
A member of a priestly line. Distinct from general rabbinic ordination.
Machloket
A dispute or controversy, including scholarly disagreement.
Machshavah
Thought; the mod’s discipline for Jewish philosophy, theology, and related intellectual literature.
Minhag
Custom or practice, often associated with a regional tradition.
Mikvah
A ritual immersion bath.
Nagid
A Jewish leadership title; the mod’s realm-wide office is distinct from local communal leadership.
Ne’eman
A trustee; one of the communal council’s officers.
Parnas
A communal leader or administrator.
Parshanut
Interpretation or commentary, especially on Scripture.
Pesak Halakha
A legal ruling or determination.
Piyyut
Liturgical poetry.
Rav / Rabbi
A rabbinic title; in the mod, associated with scholarly qualification and ordination.
Responsum; responsa
A written answer to a legal or religious question; answers collectively.
Rosh Yeshiva
The head of a yeshiva.
Rosh ha-Shmirah
The head of the communal watch.
Sefer; sefarim
A book; books.
She’elah; she’elot
A question; questions, particularly those sent for a scholarly answer.
Shochet
A ritual slaughterer.
Shtadlan
An intercessor representing the community before outside authorities.
Sofer
A scribe.
Teshuva
Repentance or return; used for reconciliation after cherem.
Tzedakah
Charity and the obligation of material support.
Yeshiva; yeshivot
An academy of advanced religious learning; academies.

These concise definitions explain the mod’s usage. Historical meanings and institutional arrangements varied by period and region.

title: Versions, evidence, and development status
summary: What the wiki covers, what is generated, and how to keep it accurate.
body:
A development wiki

The first editorial pass was reviewed on 25 November 2026. A second pass on 26 November 2026 added the 0.2.0 features and screenshots from a live session; see the Rashi playthrough. It describes implemented development features, with explicit notes where live verification remains pending. It is not a guarantee that every described addition is in the last Workshop upload.

StatusWhat it establishes
Implemented / source-builtDefinitions and logic exist in the code.
Source-checked / validator-checkedSpecified static checks passed, subject to the recorded baseline and tool limits.
Live-testedThe named scenario was exercised in the game. This does not test every save, start, or outcome.
ProposedA design exists; it should not be advertised as an available action.

Source priority

The roadmap is the primary account of current status. Implementation records explain what code actually does and where it departs from a specification. Specifications can include unbuilt proposals and superseded sections; read their status lines and later addenda.

Every authored article links to its supporting files. The wiki’s guides are summaries, not a second design specification. The generated book and building references read the checked-out mod data during each build.

Catalog dates

The book catalog reports the dates configured by the mod, including approximate or conventional datings. A date before a bookmark is a necessary chronological indication, not a promise that a copy is owned, visible, accepted, or available to every reader. Player-authored landmark substitutions can alter campaign history.

Keeping the wiki current

Edit the articles in docs/wiki/articles.json with feature changes, and update the editorial review date when the content is reviewed. Run the builder and its link checks. The Pages workflow rebuilds catalog entries from the same revision of the mod when merged to master.

Keep development notes, speculative designs, and test logs in the repository. Link to them from articles when useful, rather than copying every internal note into the player navigation.
